source_fields.instance: (f,g,x0,y0) and declared oracle law; dimensions are arbitrary finite and minimax is over them

assumptions.description: For every x and $t\in[0,\bar t]$, the lower-level minimum of $h_t=g+tf$ is finite and attained, and $\|\nabla_yh_t\|^2\ge2\mu(h_t-\min_yh_t)$ holds globally with the same mu for all x,t. This includes g at t=0 but does not follow from g being PL alone. Strong convexity and uniqueness are not required.
The function f is C_f-Lipschitz in the lower-level variable y, uniformly in x. Convexity in x and global value-Lipschitz continuity in x are not assumed.
The full gradient of $f$ is jointly $L_f$-Lipschitz in $(x,y)$, and its full Hessian is jointly $\rho_f$-Lipschitz. The constant $L$ is a common upper bound on $L_f$ and $L_g$.
The full gradient of $g$ is jointly $L_g$-Lipschitz in $(x,y)$, and its full Hessian is jointly $\rho_g=\rho$-Lipschitz. Strong convexity of g is not additionally assumed.
The optimistic objective satisfies $\Phi(x_0)-\inf_x\Phi(x)\le\Delta$, with Delta a public fixed finite initialization budget.

The initial point satisfies $\operatorname{dist}(y_0,Y^*(x_0))\le R_0$, with z0 = y0. The source solution-set perturbation bound gives an initial tracking bound from public data. Distance is measured to the solution set; no undeclared unique y* is selected.

description_paragraphs: Consider the optimistic bilevel problem $Y^*(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in\mathbb{R}^{d_y}}g(x,y)$, $\Phi(x)=\min_{y\in Y^*(x)}f(x,y)$, and seek stationarity of $\min_x\Phi(x)$. Multiple global lower-level solutions are allowed; the defining minima must be attained. Among lower-level minimizers, select one minimizing the upper-level objective.

description_paragraphs: Public inputs are dimension, target accuracy, the model's budgets, and the initial point. The original functions, their lower-level solutions, and the reduced objective are hidden. Queries are restricted to the stated interfaces; inner optima and undeclared derivatives are not available for free.
The map $(x,y)\mapsto\nabla f(x,y)$ is returned exactly, with no additional random noise.
The response is $(x,y)\longmapsto \nabla g(x,y)$, returned exactly with no additional stochastic noise.
